making_of.title: Newest episodes first
body: The official episode page, redbelly.network/ama, has Episode 29 (9 July 2026) as its newest Redbelly Insights episode. Episodes 25 to 29 were downloaded from the links on that page and read through, newest first.
A moment made the cut only if it was about Redbelly technology, Project Acacia or Tokeniser, landed one point that a newcomer can follow, and said something no other clip in the pack says.

making_of.title: No edits inside a clip
body: Each clip runs straight through from its first word to its last. Nothing is removed from the middle and nothing is stitched together, so a speaker cannot be made to say something they did not say.
In and out points sit in the silence between two words, and the audit checks each clip's audio against the episode at the listed time.

making_of.title: Subtitles checked three ways
body: Three speech models (Whisper small.en, medium.en and large-v3) each transcribed every clip. The subtitles were settled word by word against all three, and names and titles were checked on redbelly.network, tokeniser.com and each guest's company site.

Terms follow the brief: Redbelly, RBNT, Tokeniser, Project Acacia, in Australian spelling. Stammers and words like um are left out. The lines are burned in with the current word picked out in red, and also supplied as SRT.

making_of.title: The speaker stays on screen
body: Face recognition finds the speaker in each camera shot of the 16:9 episode, so the square window always sits on the person talking rather than the host. Within a shot the window does not move.
Where the episode itself shows the host for a moment while the guest talks, the guest's nearest frame is held and the sound carries on. SOURCES.md lists each of these.

making_of.title: One level for all six
body: Only the episode's own sound is used. Every clip is measured and brought to -14 LUFS, the level X, YouTube and Instagram play at, with a limiter holding true peaks below -2 dBTP, so the six play at the same volume.
Nothing has been added: no music, no effects, no outside footage.

making_of.title: In the DAO's colours
body: Clips and page use the Redbelly DAO Task Board brand kit: slate backgrounds, one red accent, Be Vietnam Pro for words, JetBrains Mono for numbers such as episode and time, and the DAO logo on dark with no plate.
Headline, name plate and captions sit above the strip at the bottom where X, Shorts, Reels and TikTok draw their own buttons.

cuts.headline: Proof of stake still gets hacked. What's missing?
cuts.person_title: Founder & Chief Science Officer, Redbelly Network
cuts.takeaway: Proof of stake chains still get hacked. Redbelly is a regulated proof of stake chain, designed so every participant has a reason to pull in the same direction instead of tech-savvy players profiting at the expense of everyday users.
cuts.post_copy: Proof of stake still gets hacked. Redbelly founder Vincent Gramoli on a regulated proof of stake chain where incentives line up, so tech-savvy players can't profit at everyday investors' expense.
cuts.transcript: So it looks like, you know, blockchain has moved and matured from proof of work that was extremely energy greedy to this proof of stake strategy that is better. But still, we can see hacks happening all the time. And now we have this regulated version of proof of stake blockchain with Redbelly. I think what is extremely important is to really find a way to incentivise all the participants to go in the right direction, the same direction, right? And not to have tech-savvy people that will profit on the back of moms and pops. So really having these kind of rationals that are captured, such that everyone is doing its best so that everyone can benefit. You know, we're lowering the barrier of entry to these economic opportunities for the masses.

cuts.headline: Stablecoins work like cash. Redbelly wallets are KYC'd.
cuts.takeaway: Tokenised bank deposits stay inside each bank, because the bank must know every holder, while stablecoins move between digital wallets like cash; with every Redbelly wallet already KYC'd, holders can choose who they transact with.
cuts.post_copy: Tokenised deposits stay inside the bank. Stablecoins move like a $50 note. Macropod CEO Drew Bradford on why it matters that every wallet on Redbelly is already KYC'd.
cuts.transcript: So anybody that holds a CBA tokenised deposit, or Westpac, or NAB, or whatever, they're going to have to do KYC: here's my utility bill, here's my passport, before that money can get sent to them, right? So tokenised deposits will live within a bank ecosphere, but they won't be free moving. So stablecoins are the notes, you know, your digital version of the $50 note, the $100, and you can send it and move it instantly. And so I see that's where they fit in the ecosphere. And anybody that has a digital wallet can take that, and you can take money off somebody, and you could set various degrees of who do I want to transact with, who don't I want to transact with, that can all get set up. As we know, all the Redbelly wallets have been KYC'd.
editor_notes: KYC means know your customer: the identity checks a bank or platform runs before it deals with someone. CBA, Westpac and NAB are Australian banks.

cuts.headline: After Project Acacia, tokenised bonds are next
cuts.takeaway: Tokenised bonds are the next step after Project Acacia: the RBA's Ellis Connolly named bonds as the first cab off the rank, and Brad Jones said the question is no longer if, but when and how.
cuts.post_copy: After Project Acacia, the RBA is pointing at tokenised bonds: not if, but when and how. Macropod CEO Drew Bradford on why this is coming.
cuts.transcript: Oh, look, we tease Brad Jones, you're not going fast enough. But look, we saw it in the budget. The only positive thing in the budget the other night was the mention of tokenised bonds, or the only positive that I talked about. So, Project Acacia, hey, you never know, it might even be out before this podcast comes out. The report, that will go through guardrails. This is where we think the market's going. Ellis Connolly, when he testified in the parliamentary economics committee, he said Project Acacia, the first cab off the rank should be bonds and tokenised bonds. Brad Jones got up the other day at the AP+ Beyond Tomorrow payments and said, you know, it's not if, it's when and how. So this is coming.
editor_notes: For the first 1.8 seconds the episode is still on the host while Drew Bradford starts to answer, so his first frame on camera is held until the episode cuts to him. The audio is unchanged.

Names checked against official sources: Brad Jones is the RBA's Assistant Governor (Financial System) and spoke at the Australian Payments Plus (AP+) Beyond Tomorrow forum; Ellis Connolly is the RBA's Head of Payments Policy. Short host back-channel words ("yeah, yeah", "fantastic") are not subtitled.

cuts.headline: Every regulated asset needs a registry. Enter Tokeniser.
cuts.takeaway: Every regulated asset needs a registry of who holds what, so Redbelly acquired the Liquidise registry business and rebranded it Tokeniser, covering origination, servicing and the registry before secondary trading.
cuts.post_copy: Who holds what? In regulated markets, everything starts with the registry. Redbelly Executive Chairman Alan Burt on why Redbelly acquired Liquidise and relaunched it as Tokeniser.
cuts.transcript: Yeah, so obviously at Redbelly, we've been always focused on how we bring financial services on chain. And Liquidise has always been a great partner of Redbelly, and they've been focused specifically at the time on private equities. We saw the opportunity at Redbelly to broaden that, and obviously focused on other alternate assets. But the key to everything is the registry. So who holds what? In a regulated environment, the bearer instrument is, other than cash, pretty much illegal now across every jurisdiction. So there is always regulatory required a registry. And so we've been working with Matt and saw the opportunity with some of our other partners to greatly accelerate that adoption by helping them with already having a tokenised registry. So as Matt said, we've acquired Liquidise, the registry business and their customers, and we've now rebranded that into Tokeniser, which is much more focused on a full cradle to grave, if you like, on asset origination, asset servicing and obviously registry, and then what everyone wants to hear about, the secondary trading opportunities that will be unlocked. But we've got to start with, let's get the assets on.
editor_notes: Subtitle decision at 27 s: the three transcription models split between "regularly" and "regulatory" required. The subtitle follows large-v3 and the sense of the sentence, which is about what regulation requires.

cuts.headline: What Project Acacia tested inside a real fund
cuts.takeaway: In Project Acacia, Tokeniser used a real fund, with TAF Capital as trustee and Macropod's AUDM stablecoin for settlement, to run subscriptions, distributions and redemptions in fully tokenised form.
cuts.post_copy: A real fund, a real stablecoin, three everyday fund processes. Tokeniser's Matt Mills on what Project Acacia tested, and why tokenised fund processes are quicker, safer and more transparent.
cuts.transcript: So Tokeniser had the privilege of also being involved in Project Acacia. We had the benefit of working with both the trustee, TAF Capital, who were fantastic partners in letting us essentially use one of their funds as a guinea pig for the purpose of Project Acacia, and Macropod, who supplied and provided the AUD stablecoin, AUDM, infrastructure for which we could settle against any transactions. So one of the cool things that Tokeniser did was essentially, as rightly pointed out, tackle some of those processes and payments in a fully tokenised fashion. And the goal was to demonstrate just how much quicker, safer and more transparent those processes would be in a tokenised fashion versus a traditional style. So to give an example, we tried to essentially conduct three normal, common processes that exist in any fund. Those were the subscriptions: how does an investor acquire the units? They were the distributions and the redemptions.
editor_notes: For the first 0.7 seconds the episode is still on the host while Matt Mills starts to answer, so his first frame on camera is held until the episode cuts to him. The audio is unchanged.
TAF Capital was the trustee of the Project Acacia fund, and Macropod issues the AUDM stablecoin used for settlement.

cuts.headline: What investors see when they log in to Tokeniser
cuts.takeaway: Tokeniser gives investors a familiar web portal: log in, see holdings and their value, download statements and certificates and receive announcements, which makes the issuer look serious and puts investors first.
cuts.post_copy: Log in, see your holdings, download your statements. Tokeniser's Matt Mills on why tokenised assets should feel like a modern investor portal, and why investors are the real customers.
cuts.transcript: And from a user experience, it's very much that traditional web experience. You get invited to view your holdings in a particular company or fund. You register an account, you log in and have a dashboard where you can see your holdings, see the value of those holdings. You can download statements, whether they're holding statements, share certificates, unit certificates, receive communications in the form of announcements or communications from the company or funds. And what's nice about that, and the user feedback we've gotten from our existing clients, has been that it's modern, it's fast, and most importantly, it looks and makes the issuer look serious, and shows that they care about the investor experience. And that's something that really matters to us, because we know that at the end of the day, even though it's the trustees or the companies that pay our fees and subscribe or use the product, they're doing it for the benefit of their investors. And we know our real customers are those investors, and getting a really good experience.
editor_notes: From 49.8 s to 52.1 s of the clip (episode 24:03.5 to 24:05.9) the episode cuts away from Matt Mills, so his last frame is held with a slow push-in while the audio carries on.
